overview: In the thirteenth century, Cham rulers governed several coastal and river-valley centers in what is now central and southern Vietnam. Their alliances, rivalries and temple networks crossed the neat divisions suggested by a map. This card focuses on the atlas’s 1200 to 1279 interval, separately from the longer Champa history. Neither endpoint marks its founding or disappearance. The coarse imported outline even omits relevant coastal places such as Po Nagar at Nha Trang; it cannot establish precise borders or a single unified state.

periods.title: Coastal powers and political recovery
periods.summary: The atlas interval covers Khmer intervention, renewed Cham royal claims and active river-mouth centers.

items.text: Champa’s important centers grew beside rivers and useful sea approaches. Around Quy Nhon, temple remains belong especially to the eleventh through thirteenth centuries. Vickery also identifies apparently competing royal claims in 1244. A king’s boast about ruling all Champa therefore needs checking against the inscriptions of other rulers.

The Phan Rang inscription C4 recalls Khmer departure for Angkor and Cham movement to Vijaya in 1220/1. It then records a royal consecration in 1226/7 and renewed temples. This is a ruler’s account of restoration after warfare, preserved on a sandstone doorway.

The same doorway lists named rice fields dedicated to Svayamutpanna, including fields bounded by a dyke. It also records gold and silver. Religious institutions depended on agricultural resources as well as impressive buildings; these inscriptions preserve the accounting behind royal generosity.

At Po Nagar in Nha Trang, a thirteenth-century inscription lists 55 enslaved people alongside temple property. They include Cham, Khmer, Paganese and Siamese people. This stark record shows that temples could command coerced labor, and that political and commercial connections also moved people against their will.

Zhao Rugua’s account, compiled around 1225 from reports and earlier texts, describes officials boarding merchant ships. They recorded cargo in white characters on folded black material, translated as leather. Goods were inspected before unloading, and the government claimed two tenths. Even a sea voyage ended with paperwork.

The same account describes ploughing with two buffaloes and lists beans, millet, sugar cane, bananas and coconuts. Scented wood cut in the mountains was taxed before private trading. Farming and forest products both supported exchanges with overseas merchants.

Zhao reports frequent bathing, fragrant body preparations and clothing perfumed with scented smoke. He also describes a procession of fishing boats in the fourth lunar month. These are reported customs, not proof that every household washed or celebrated identically, and they do not establish a sewer or toilet system.

For Panduranga around Phan Rang, Zhao describes palm-leaf roofs and protective wooden palisades. That short account offers a glimpse of ordinary dwellings alongside the region’s surviving stone and brick monuments.

sections.title: Discoveries and a sentence carved in stone

items.text: At Thap Mam in Binh Dinh, excavation in 1934 uncovered tower foundations inside a walled compound and a reported 58 tons of stone sculpture and architectural decoration. The complex is dated to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Its remains helped scholars define a distinctive sculptural style; another excavation followed in 2011.

One earlier masterpiece from Thap Mam, dated to the twelfth century, is a sandstone dragon with raised hind legs and a gem in its mouth. The museum guide suggests a combination with the Hindu sea creature makara. Artists could combine familiar creatures into something entirely new: quite a balancing act in stone.

C4, dated 1226/7 at Phan Rang, reads “humā parik· 155 jāk·”: “the rice-fields of Parik: 155 jāk.” This is the editors’ Latin transliteration of Old Cham, not a reproduction of its carved script. The land unit jāk is left unconverted.

Domestic archaeology is harder to date than famous temple sculptures. In his 2022 research overview, archaeologist William Southworth stresses how limited the ceramic sequence after the fourth century still is. A potsherd can be real evidence while its date remains uncertain. These sources do not establish thirteenth-century school routines, medical treatments or household toilets.

Champa was still a political actor after 1279. In 1283, Khubilai Khan demanded passage and supplies from the Tran rulers of Dai Viet for a campaign against their southern neighbor. They refused. The ensuing wars connected Cham, Vietnamese and Mongol decisions, rather than ending neatly when this atlas layer changes.

Living Cham communities also remain. UNESCO’s 2022 pottery record describes women shaping household vessels by walking around them instead of turning a wheel. Pots stay put while the potter moves! This is documented modern craft, not proof that the same technique made every medieval Cham vessel.

In that modern practice, children learn through hands-on family teaching, while women exchange skills and conversation during work. Unglazed vessels are fired outdoors with wood and straw for seven to eight hours at about 800°C. Keeping a craft alive involves everyday practice, materials and livelihoods as well as preserving museum objects.

ending.text: The map’s 1279 cutoff is not Champa’s fall: it remained involved in regional diplomacy and warfare afterward. Later political losses require their own dates and local histories. Cham communities and living crafts continue, without implying that their present practices are unchanged copies of thirteenth-century life.
